Monitor Tester is an open web utility designed to assist users in visually evaluating display panels using browser-renderable test patterns, motion simulations, and client-side calculations. These tests are intended for visual screening and self-diagnosis.
Not a Replacement for Hardware Colorimeters

Browser-based software cannot replace physical spectrophotometers, hardware colorimeters (such as Calibrite or Datacolor Spyder), or optical oscilloscopes. Monitor Tester does not generate ICC color profiles, read physical photometric nits, or certify absolute color accuracy (Delta-E).

Monitor Tester is provided on an 'AS IS' and 'AS AVAILABLE' basis without warranties of any kind, whether express or implied. While we strive for precision, test results may vary based on operating system display scaling, GPU driver configurations, browser hardware acceleration, and ambient lighting conditions.

Display manufacturers enforce their own specific warranty terms regarding pixel defects (such as ISO 9241-307 Class 1 or Class 2 standards, which often define minimum thresholds of stuck or dead subpixels before an RMA is authorized). Identifying a defect on Monitor Tester does not automatically guarantee warranty replacement by your device manufacturer.
The underlying source code of Monitor Tester is licensed under the open-source MIT License. You are free to inspect, review, and fork the source code in accordance with the license.
Have feedback, found a display discrepancy, or want to suggest a new test pattern? Here are the best ways to reach the project.
Report bugs, browser rendering issues, or request new display test patterns on our public GitHub repository.
Monitor Tester is open source. Pull requests for test improvements, performance optimizations, and translation corrections are warmly welcomed.
For general inquiries, collaborations, or private feedback regarding the project, feel free to reach out directly via email.

Test monitor ability to render neutral grays without color tinting.
Assess color vibrancy and detect banding in high-saturation gradients.
Tune your monitor's black levels to ensure dark details aren't crushed.
Tune your monitor's contrast to ensure bright details aren't clipped.
Visually estimate your monitor's gamma tracking (target 2.2 for sRGB).
Verify your browser and OS correctly detect HDR and Wide Color Gamut.
This test renders a pure black screen. It is designed to expose backlight bleed, clouding, or IPS glow that typically affects LCD/LED panels.

Unlike a dead pixel (which is permanently black), a stuck pixel is a single subpixel (red, green, or blue) that is permanently turned on. Sometimes, rapidly cycling colors can un-stick the liquid crystal.
This test displays stepped grayscale backgrounds to help identify backlight bleeding, edge darkening (vignetting), and Dirty Screen Effect (DSE).
This test helps you configure your monitor's black level (brightness) setting. It displays extremely dark shades near pure black.
Turn off room lights or reduce glare on the screen.
Adjust your monitor's 'Brightness' setting until you can barely distinguish block 1 from the pure black background.
If blocks 1-5 look identical to the background, your blacks are being crushed.
This test helps you configure your monitor's white level (contrast) setting. It displays extremely bright shades near pure white.
Adjust your monitor's 'Contrast' setting until you can distinguish block 254 from the pure white background.
If blocks 250-254 look identical to the background, your whites are clipping.
Do not set contrast so high that bright details are lost.
This test displays neutral grayscale backgrounds. It helps you check if your monitor suffers from unwanted color tints in its gray rendering.
Cycle through the gray levels using Space or right arrow.
Look for pink, blue, or green tints in what should be neutral gray.
Use your monitor's RGB balance controls to correct any color cast.
This test displays a continuous color spectrum and stepped saturation blocks for primary colors.
Check the smooth spectrum for obvious banding or harsh transitions.
Look at the individual saturation steps to ensure distinct differences between blocks.
Adjust your monitor's saturation/vibrancy settings if colors look washed out or overly neon.
This tool helps you estimate your monitor's physical gamma curve. A gamma of 2.2 is the standard for sRGB and Windows PCs.
Enter fullscreen and move away from the monitor, or squint your eyes until the top lines blur into a solid gray.
Compare the blurred top half to the three solid blocks below.
The block that perfectly matches the brightness of the blurred top half indicates your monitor's approximate gamma.
ABOUT THIS TEST: This tool relies on visual perception and standard browser color rendering. It is not a replacement for a hardware colorimeter.
Assess how well your monitor handles fast motion without blurring or smearing details.
Track the moving blocks with your eyes.
Look at the small inner square. If the edges blur completely, your monitor has a slow pixel response time.
Adjust speed and contrast to test under different panel overdrive scenarios.
This tool queries your browser's APIs to determine if High Dynamic Range (HDR) and Wide Color Gamut (P3) are currently enabled and supported by your display chain.
If it says 'Not Supported' but your monitor is HDR-capable, ensure HDR is turned on in Windows/macOS display settings.
Ensure you are using a modern browser with hardware acceleration enabled.

View the screen from extreme angles.
Watch the moving bar for horizontal tearing.
Look for faint outlines of static elements.
Look for halos around the bright square.
Draw all over the screen to check for dead zones.
Verify skin tones and natural colors.
Use a camera at high shutter speed.
Check if the colors in the center match or blend with the outer ring.

Also called CSS resolution, this is the grid your browser uses to render content. OS scaling and browser zoom can make this lower than your physical panel resolution.
The physical pixel grid built into your display panel. Running at non-native resolutions involves scaling and can make text appear softer.
DPR is how many physical device pixels are used to draw a single CSS pixel. A DPR of 2 means a 10x10 CSS box uses 20x20 physical pixels.
Pixel density (PPI) describes how many pixels are packed into each inch of the display. Higher PPI means sharper text and images, assuming the viewing distance is the same.
Higher resolution increases rendering workload. Higher refresh rate increases frame delivery requirements. The available combination depends on your GPU, connection bandwidth, and display.
My resolution is lower than expected.
Check OS display scaling (e.g., 150%). This reduces the logical resolution reported to the browser. Also check browser zoom settings.
Check that the OS output is set to 4K. If you are mirroring a lower-resolution laptop screen, the external monitor will look blurry.
Check your cable. Some high resolution + high refresh combinations require DisplayPort 1.4 or HDMI 2.1. Older cables may limit you to 60Hz.

Browser frame timing is affected by system load, power saving, background tabs, and browser behavior. It is an approximation, not a direct hardware query.

Monitor Tester is designed with a strict privacy-first architecture. All display diagnostic tests and calculations execute entirely inside your local browser.

When you visit Monitor Tester and run display tests, we do NOT collect, transmit, or store any personal data, hardware serial numbers, diagnostic observations, or screen metrics on external servers. There are no backend tracking databases, user accounts, or login requirements.
To provide convenient features such as checklist tracking and defect marker coordinates, Monitor Tester utilizes your browser's private local storage APIs:

Active Session & Observations (localStorage): Stores your self-reported test ratings (Pass, Check, Issue), custom notes, and pixel defect pin coordinates (X/Y pixels) so your report remains accessible if you refresh the page.

Workflow Queue (sessionStorage): Temporarily keeps track of your current step in guided inspection workflows (e.g., General Checkup or Used Monitor Inspection). This is automatically cleared when you close your browser tab.
You can clear all stored data at any time by clicking 'Reset' in the test runner, clearing your browser's site data, or using your browser's private / incognito browsing mode.
Monitor Tester does not use third-party advertising cookies, behavioral trackers, or marketing pixels. The site does not sell, rent, or monetize your browsing activity.

Monitor Tester requests only the standard Fullscreen API permission when you choose to enter full-screen testing mode. Fullscreen requires an explicit user gesture (such as clicking the Fullscreen button or pressing 'F') as enforced by your browser. We never request camera, microphone, notification, or geographic location permissions.
A free, privacy-first browser utility built to evaluate, inspect, and troubleshoot computer monitors, laptops, mobile devices, and TVs without software installation.

Buying a new or used monitor often involves uncertainty: dead pixels, backlight bleed, washed-out contrast, and ghosting are difficult to identify during brief in-store checks or unboxings. Monitor Tester was created to provide a complete, accessible suite of diagnostic patterns that anyone can run immediately in any modern web browser.

Every test runs locally on your device using standard HTML5 Canvas, WebGL, CSS hardware acceleration, and the Screen and Window APIs. No downloads, native installers, or administrative permissions are needed. Your display data stays entirely on your computer.
Detect dead pixels, stuck subpixels, bright subpixels, and panel image retention (burn-in) across pure color fields.
Evaluate continuous gradients, color banding steps, color gamut boundaries, and multi-step grayscale ramps.
Tune near-black and near-white clipping, check dark-room backlight bleeding, and assess full-screen brightness uniformity.
Check ghosting trails, evaluate pixel overdrive settings, measure V-Sync refresh rate (Hz), and inspect for screen tearing.
Inspect detected screen metrics (DPR, color depth), calculate PPI and optimal viewing distances, compare displays, and test multi-touch.
Monitor Tester is an open-source project. You can inspect the source code, report rendering bugs, suggest new test patterns, or contribute directly on GitHub.
